chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Ibn Abi Umayr, who said:
Isa ibn A'yn, when he performed Hajj, would turn to supplication for his brothers until the people would depart.

It was said to him: 'You spend your wealth and tire your body, and when you reach the place where needs are presented to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, you turn to supplication for your brothers and leave your own self?'
He said: 'I am confident in the angel's call for me, but doubtful in the supplication for my own self.'

key_terms.الْمَوْقِفِ: The standing place (Mawqif), specifically referring to the place of standing during Hajj rituals
key_terms.تُبَثُّ: To be presented or poured forth (referring to needs being presented to God)
key_terms.يُفِيضَ: To depart or disperse (referring to the crowd leaving)

ai.seo_question: Why did Isa ibn A'yn prioritize praying for others over himself during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the spiritual humility of Isa ibn A'yn, who prioritized interceding for the community during the critical moment of standing at Arafat, reflecting the Shia emphasis on self-effacement (*fana*) in divine presence. His rationale—trusting the angelic call for his own needs while doubting his personal supplication's efficacy—underscores the scholarly view that sincere, humble prayer for others is often more accepted than self-centered pleas. This practice aligns with the concept of *istishhad* (seeking witness) by angels, reinforcing the communal aspect of Hajj rituals in Shia jurisprudence.
